prompt: Which role does the Scrum Guide give the person who tests?
hint: Look at the third row of the table.

choices.text: Quality owner
choices.why: There are three accountabilities and this is not one of them.

choices.text: A fourth accountability beside the Scrum Master
choices.why: There are three, and the Guide keeps it that way on purpose.

choices.text: Developer
choices.why: Right: everyone who builds the increment is a Developer, whatever their specialism.

choices.text: Tester
choices.why: The Guide names no such role.

prompt: Why does the Scrum Guide leave out a separate testing role?

choices.text: The Guide was written before testing was a profession of its own, in 1985
choices.why: The first Guide is from 2010, and testing was a profession long before.

choices.text: The team answers for the increment together
choices.why: Right: no sub-group can be accountable for "the testing" of it.

choices.text: Scrum teams do not test
choices.why: They test; the Guide just gives testing no separate owner.

choices.text: Testing is the Scrum Master’s job
choices.why: The Scrum Master answers for the team’s effectiveness, not for testing.

prompt: Match each artefact to its commitment.
How many events does Scrum have, counting the sprint itself?
hint: The sprint contains the other four.

prompt: A team follows every rule of the Scrum Guide and still ships the Wednesday defect. How is that possible?
hint: What does the Guide say about how to test?

choices.text: Scrum says nothing about how to test
choices.why: Right: it is a frame for inspecting work, and it helps as much as the team is honest.

choices.text: The team must have skipped the daily scrum
choices.why: The question says every rule was followed.

choices.text: Scrum forbids testing combinations of discounts
choices.why: It forbids nothing of the kind.

choices.text: The sprint was longer than a month, which the Guide does not allow for any team
choices.why: Nothing in the question says so.

prompt: At planning for coupons, Lia asked whether a coupon combines with the Wednesday discount. Nobody knew. What did the team do?

choices.text: Asked Lia to decide
choices.why: A price rule is the product owner’s decision.

choices.text: Dropped coupons
choices.why: Coupons went ahead, on their own.

choices.text: Split the story and left the combination for Joana to decide
choices.why: Right: coupons alone now, the combination next sprint.

choices.text: Built both and tested later
choices.why: That is how the question would have become a defect.

prompt: What does the tester bring to sprint planning, by this lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the four questions of lesson 2
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: how the story will be tested
choices.why: Yes: it can change the estimate.

choices.text: the combinations with stories already built
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: a list of the defects each developer caused last sprint
choices.why: No: that is blame, and planning looks forward.

prompt: On day seven three stories are waiting for Lia. Which event is where the team should notice?

choices.text: Planning for the next sprint
choices.why: Too late for these three stories.

choices.text: The daily scrum
choices.why: Right: saying what waits for testing shows the mini-waterfall forming.

choices.text: The sprint review, when the stories are shown
choices.why: By then the sprint is over.

choices.text: The retrospective
choices.why: Useful afterwards; the daily catches it while it can still change.

prompt: In the quadrants of lesson 11, where does the sprint review sit?

choices.text: Q2
choices.why: Q2 supports the team with examples before the code.

choices.text: Q4
choices.why: Q4 is the technology-facing critique: speed, load, security.

choices.text: Q3
choices.why: Right: people trying the product and reacting to it.

choices.text: Q1
choices.why: Q1 is unit checks that support the team.

prompt: After the 9:30 Sunday, which question did the retrospective ask?

choices.text: How many customers were overcharged?
choices.why: Worth knowing, and it says nothing about the process.

choices.text: Should Lia have tested more?
choices.why: The defect was possible before testing began.

choices.text: Why was it possible?
choices.why: Right: the answer was that nobody asked who types the session times.

choices.text: Who wrote the line that compared the time as text?
choices.why: That finds somebody to blame and changes nothing.

prompt: Rafael says "done" and means the code is written. Lia says "done" and means she tested it. What fixes this?

choices.text: A shared definition of done
choices.why: Right: the same written bar for every story.

choices.text: Letting the Scrum Master decide case by case
choices.why: Then "done" means what one person thinks that day.

choices.text: More detailed acceptance criteria
choices.why: Those are per story; this disagreement is about every story.

choices.text: A longer sprint
choices.why: Length does not settle what "done" means.

prompt: What separates the definition of done from acceptance criteria?

choices.text: Criteria are written by testers
choices.why: They are usually written by the product owner, often with the team.

choices.text: The definition is written by the product owner and the criteria by the developers who build the story
choices.why: The definition belongs to the team.

choices.text: The definition applies to every story; criteria to one
choices.why: Right: one bar for all, and what this story has to do.

choices.text: They are the same thing with two names
choices.why: They are often confused, and they differ.

prompt: A story passes all its acceptance criteria. Nobody explored it, and an old check now fails. Is it done?

choices.text: No
choices.why: Right: lines 3 and 4 of the definition are not met.

choices.text: Yes: the criteria are what the story has to do
choices.why: A story meets both, or it is not done.

choices.text: Yes, if the product owner accepts it in the review
choices.why: The definition of done comes before the review.

choices.text: Only if the failing check is fixed next sprint
choices.why: That is lesson 11’s test debt.

prompt: A story fails the definition of done on the last day. What is the honest outcome?
hint: It is not shown as finished.

choices.text: Ask Lia to sign it off
choices.why: Her job is to keep the definition honest, not to waive it.

choices.text: It is not done, and goes back to the backlog or stays in progress
choices.why: Right: and it is not shown at the review as finished.

choices.text: Call it done and fix it next sprint
choices.why: That is the dishonest outcome, and test debt.

choices.text: Remove the failing line from the definition
choices.why: That can be discussed at the retrospective, not on the last day to pass one story.

prompt: Put the lines of the Cine Aurora definition of done in the order the team wrote them.
items: each acceptance criterion has a passing test
the old automated checks still pass
every question has a written answer
in a version that could ship today
trap: Each line exists because something went wrong; the order follows the work.

prompt: Which version of the criterion for older customers can a tester use?
hint: Prices and both sides of the line.

choices.text: Older customers are happy
choices.why: Nobody can check that before release.

choices.text: 59 pays R$ 36,00; 60 and 61 pay R$ 18,00, evening
choices.why: Right: three checks with their expected results.

choices.text: Customers over 60 pay half
choices.why: Exactly the sentence that hid the defect.

choices.text: The discount works correctly
choices.why: Correct according to what?

prompt: Why does writing a criterion as examples help the product owner as much as the tester?
hint: Can Joana write "60 pays R$ 18,00" without deciding?

choices.text: Examples are shorter
choices.why: The examples version was the longest of the three.

choices.text: Examples replace the definition of done
choices.why: They are per story; the definition is for all.

choices.text: Examples let the developers skip writing tests for the story
choices.why: Each example becomes a test.

choices.text: An example forces each ambiguity into the open
choices.why: Right: she has to decide whether sixty counts.

prompt: Given a customer aged 60 at a Thursday evening session, when they buy a ticket, ___ they pay R$ 18,00.
Which part of Given/When/Then does a tester need most?

choices.text: Then
choices.why: Right: the format makes it hard to leave out.

choices.text: Given
choices.why: It sets up the situation; the expected result is elsewhere.

choices.text: When
choices.why: It is the action.

choices.text: The title of the story
choices.why: Not part of the format.

prompt: Joana has written criteria for "older customers pay half". Which of these is the tester adding? Choose all that apply.
hint: Edges, combinations, inputs, what happens after.

choices.text: a customer aged 59 and one aged 60
choices.why: Yes: both sides of the line.

choices.text: an older customer on a Wednesday
choices.why: Yes: a combination.

choices.text: an age typed as a word
choices.why: Yes: an input nobody mentioned.

choices.text: a criterion that the code be written in Python
choices.why: No: that says nothing about what the story has to do.

prompt: The team keeps calling stories done that break old checks. Where does the tester take the gap?
hint: The event that looks at how the team works.

choices.text: The daily scrum
choices.why: Fifteen minutes about progress toward the goal.

choices.text: Straight to the product owner, in private
choices.why: The definition belongs to the whole team.

choices.text: A defect report against each developer who called a story done
choices.why: That is policing, and the lesson asks for honesty instead.

choices.text: The retrospective
choices.why: Right: the team decides whether the definition or the sprint was wrong.
